params.text:
Look for causes, not culprits

Reporting an incident is only worthwhile if something is learned from it; the purpose is to learn, not to punish. After a serious or recurring incident, your service will investigate to understand what happened and why. A good investigation looks for the root cause — the underlying reason — rather than for someone to blame. Most incidents come from a chain of factors such as staffing, training, equipment, procedures or communication, not simply one careless person.

In a just, no-blame culture, staff feel safe to report honestly, including their own mistakes, because they know the aim is to prevent harm rather than to punish. The questions to ask are “What happened and why?” and “How do we stop it happening again?” — not “Whose fault is it?”

Changing practice and protecting records

Learning must change practice: updating a care plan, repairing or replacing equipment, revising a procedure or arranging training. Consider Mrs Okafor, who was given another resident’s tablets. The investigation found the two had similar names and the medication trolley was crowded and rushed at breakfast. The service added photographs to the medication records and calmed the morning routine — a change that protects everyone, prompted by one honest report.

Openness is also a legal duty: under the duty of candour (Regulation 20), providers must be honest with people and their families when something goes wrong and causes certain harm — telling them what happened, apologising, and explaining what will be done.

Accident and incident records often contain personal and health information. Under data protection law (UK GDPR) this information must be:

  • Kept secure — stored so that only authorised people can access it.
  • Shared only on a need-to-know basis with those who have a legitimate reason.
  • Accurate, relevant and kept no longer than necessary.

Being confidential does not mean hiding what happened from the people affected — the duty of candour still applies. It means handling the records responsibly and respecting people’s privacy.

params.alt: A care worker, beside the heading “Look for causes, not culprits”. Key points: Learn, don’t blame; Find the root cause; Report honestly, even mistakes.

params.question: Your service uses a ‘no-blame’ approach to incident reporting. What does this mean in practice?

answers.text: Staff are encouraged to report incidents and their own mistakes honestly, so the real causes can be found and put right, rather than facing automatic punishment.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A no-blame culture is about honest reporting and finding root causes; it makes services safer by helping mistakes come to light.

answers.text: Nobody is ever accountable, and even serious misconduct is simply ignored.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. No-blame does not remove accountability for genuine misconduct; it removes the fear that stops honest reporting of ordinary mistakes.

answers.text: Incidents are recorded but never investigated, so that staff are not upset.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Incidents are still investigated; the point is to learn from them and change practice, not to avoid looking at them.

answers.text: Only managers may report incidents, so that frontline staff are shielded from blame.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Everyone is encouraged to report; limiting reporting to managers would hide exactly the events the service needs to learn from.

params.question: Which statement best reflects a healthy reporting culture in adult social care?

answers.text: Staff report events openly, including their own errors, and the service investigates to learn and prevent recurrence.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Openness plus learning is the heart of a just, no-blame culture that keeps people safer.

answers.text: Staff only report events they are certain will not get them into trouble.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: No. Fear of blame hides risks. A just culture encourages honest reporting so lessons are learned.

answers.text: Records are shared freely with anyone to show how transparent the service is.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: No. Openness with those affected is right, but records still contain personal data and must be kept confidential and secure.

answers.text: The main aim of an investigation is to identify who to discipline.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: No. The aim is to understand causes and prevent recurrence, not to find someone to blame.
